entries.title: Axial Seamount
paragraphs: Axial Seamount is a basaltic submarine volcano about 480 km off the Oregon coast, sitting where the Cobb hotspot passes beneath the Juan de Fuca Ridge. That combination -- a hotspot's steady magma supply layered onto a spreading ridge -- makes it the most active, most closely watched submarine volcano in the northeast Pacific.

Its summit holds an unusually shaped rectangular caldera, about 3 km by 8 km, bounded by faults with as much as 150 m of relief; the caldera floor is roughly 50 m deeper on its north side than its south. The shallowest grid cell on this tile is about 1,392 m deep, on the summit high, close to the 1,410 m summit depth published for the volcano.

Axial has erupted at least three times since routine monitoring began: January 1998, April 2011 and April 2015. Each event is tracked by seafloor pressure and tilt instruments that catch the volcano visibly deflating as magma drains out beneath it, then slowly re-inflating over the following years -- the basis for the eruption forecasts described later in this guide.

facts.value: about 1,410 m (published); shallowest grid cell ~1,392 m

entries.title: Mushroom and Inferno
paragraphs: The ASHES (Axial Seamount Hydrothermal Emissions Study) vent field sits near the base of the caldera's western wall. OOI lists its monitored site at 45.9337°N, 130.0139°W and 1,552 m depth; this terrain grid reads about 1,540 m there. Mushroom and Inferno sit roughly 10 m apart.

Mushroom is a roughly 4 m sulfide chimney with several discharge points. OOI footage shows clear flow as well as small active black-smoker chimlets, so one chimney can carry more than one kind of discharge. The cabled observatory’s HD camera watches the chimney and the animals around it.
Inferno is a black smoker with dense animal communities on its metal-sulfide walls. Tube worms and palm worms occupy surfaces where hot vent fluids mix with cold seawater.
Most hydrothermal activity is concentrated in an area about 60-80 m across. Individual chimneys need much finer mapping than this tile's 43 × 61 m grid cells.

entries.title: Hell, Phoenix, Virgin and Virgin Mound
paragraphs: ASHES holds several smaller sulfide structures beyond Mushroom and Inferno, all generally under 4 m tall with multiple narrow discharge orifices: Hell, Phoenix and Virgin. A separate, much smaller feature, Virgin Mound, is a sub-metre anhydrite spire venting some of the most CO2-rich fluid found anywhere in the caldera.
Look east of Mushroom for the smaller-chimney scan marker.

entries.title: Life on the chimneys
paragraphs: Chemosynthetic microbes use chemicals in vent fluid to produce organic matter, supporting ASHES's animal communities. University of Washington imagery documents Ridgeia tube worms, palm worms, sulfide worms, limpets, scale worms and spider crabs. The animals occupy surfaces where vent fluids mix with cold seawater.
Filamentous bacteria coat surfaces around the vents. The field description reports rare clams at diffusely venting fractures, while chimney communities lack clams.

entries.title: The caldera's western wall
paragraphs: ASHES sits close to the base of the caldera's western boundary fault, the scarp that marks the edge of the collapsed summit. On this tile's real bathymetry, the seabed rises steadily from about 1,540 m at the vent field to around 1,416 m only 300 m to the west, consistent with the toe of that wall.

The fault trace itself -- described in the literature as roughly 130 m west of ASHES -- is finer than this tile's ~43 x 61 m grid cells can resolve individually, so this POI marks the real, surveyed rising terrain rather than a specific fault line.

entries.title: A resurfaced caldera floor
paragraphs: Axial's caldera floor has been resurfaced by lava during its recorded eruptions in 1998, 2011 and 2015. The 2015 eruption was detected in real time by the seafloor cabled observatory.

This POI sits on a broad, shallow rise on the caldera floor south of ASHES, about 1,460 m deep against roughly 1,530-1,540 m on the surrounding floor -- the kind of low, hummocky high left behind by a lava flow. No source maps this specific rise to one dated eruption, so it is described here as caldera-floor lava terrain in general rather than attributed to a single flow.

entries.title: Forecasting the next eruption
paragraphs: Axial Seamount inflates as magma accumulates beneath the caldera, then deflates abruptly during eruptions: about 3.2 m in 1998 and 2.4 m in 2011. Bill Chadwick and Scott Nooner used this pattern to forecast eruptions. NOAA identifies the April 2011 eruption as the first successfully forecast submarine eruption. In September 2014, the researchers forecast another eruption by the end of 2015; it began on 24 April 2015, about seven months after that forecast.
Pressure sensors, tiltmeters and earthquake recordings let scientists follow the volcano as it refills. An eruption forecast changes as those measurements change; inflation alone is not a countdown.

entries.title: The caldera rim and cabled observatory
paragraphs: A summit-high reference point on this tile reads about 1,395 m, close to the published 1,410 m summit depth. The tile's shallowest grid cell is about 1,392 m. The caldera's bounding faults have as much as 150 m of relief.

The University of Washington operates the Ocean Observatories Initiative's Regional Cabled Array at Axial. Seafloor instruments send seismic, pressure, temperature and chemistry measurements to shore; the ASHES camera sends HD video on a scheduled imaging cycle. These observations help scientists follow changes in the volcano and its hydrothermal system.
